title: TEDM: Time Series Forecasting with Elucidated Diffusion Models
claim: A denoiser trained on structured-noise corruption yields a score function that forecasts by integrating a differential equation along physical time.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; vertical denoising stack beside branching ODE/SDE outputs
description: Panel (a), on the left, is a vertical stack of labeled time-series traces. A black signal and a red structured-noise trace combine into a dark-red corrupted signal. A gray arrow leads to a green Denoiser box, labeled Neural network, and another arrow leads to a black denoised signal. Panel (b), on the right, shows the same Denoiser box with an arrow down to a pink Score function box. From it a line branches into two arrows, ODE on top and SDE on the bottom. The ODE output shows a black given series continuing into an orange forecast. A shaded gray inset shows successive Euler steps, with traces shifting from dark brown to orange along a gradient arrow labeled Diffusion across physical time. The SDE output shows a forecast with a light orange uncertainty band.
caption: (a) Denoising signals corrupted with structured noise. (b) TEDM uses score-based generative modeling to forecast time series by numerical integration of an ordinary (ODE) or stochastic (SDE) differential equation. The main characteristic of TEDM is reducing the physical time and the diffusion time to the same axis, as we support by theory.
abstract: Score-based generative modeling through differential equations has driven breakthroughs in high-fidelity image synthesis, offering modular model design and efficient sampling. However, this success has not been widely translated to timeseries forecasting yet. This gap stems from the sequential nature of time series, in contrast to the unordered structure of images. Here, we extend the theoretical formulation used for images to explicitly address sequential structures. We propose a diffusion-based forecasting framework (TEDM) that adapts score estimation to temporal settings and elucidates its design space. Such a design allows empirical computation of noise and signal scaling directly from data, avoiding external schedules. Notably, this reduces sampling complexity to linear in the forecast horizon. Without elaborate preprocessing, TEDM sets new state-of-the-art results on multiple forecasting benchmarks. These results illustrate the growing potential of diffusion models beyond vision. TEDM generates low-latency forecasts using a lightweight architecture, making it ideal for real-time deployment.
